title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under the frozen preregistered contract (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) we ran N = 300 matched intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) using a shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one initial LLM candidate per pair replayed to both arms) with declared model gpt-5-mini and two deterministic validators combined via logical OR. Execution completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); the repair step was never invoked because validators reported no forbidden reachability. Paired risk-difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. A one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate is ≈ 0.00994. Because the repair path was not exercised, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this run; the empirical contribution is deterministic execution accounting, a numeric bound on undetected violations under the chosen contract, and artifact-grounded design lessons for follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths.

sections.introduction: LLMs can produce intent-driven network configurations that accelerate NetOps tasks, but they also risk introducing security-relevant misconfigurations (e.g., expanding unintended reachability or violating access-control intentions). Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. We preregistered and ran a paired, deterministic experiment to address a focused operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? The preregistered design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) fixed N = 300 matched intents and a concrete adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate) to conserve model calls while preserving deterministic accounting. Our contributions are: (1) a confirmatory, preregistered paired execution with full deterministic accounting and archived per-episode validator traces; (2) a concise, artifact-grounded empirical result (n11 = 300) and a numeric upper bound (≈0.00994) on undetected baseline violations under the chosen contract; (3) a technical clarification of what the experiment does and does not test (notably, repair efficacy is untestable here because the repair path was never triggered); and (4) artifact-grounded design lessons and reproducibility pointers to guide follow-up stress tests that exercise repair behavior.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness for code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to steer repairs; these systems show verifier quality and repair strategy are decisive for realized gains (TerraFormer and related verifier-feedback approaches) [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Surveys and recent NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and consistently recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Emulation and testbed work demonstrates that execution-based validation is feasible for research evaluations, but it also highlights external-validity gaps when porting results to production networks [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. Our study complements these works by providing a preregistered, deterministically executed paired design and by archiving per-episode validator traces and provider-call accounting to support reproducible follow-up tests.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: We preregistered a paired binary design (study id cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds paired with 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in proportions of intents yielding forbidden reachability). Planned confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided (alpha = 0.05); prespecified CI method: bootstrap percentile. The preregistration and execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To limit provider usage, the run used a shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each matched intent pair a single initial LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This choice produced exactly one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) rather than independent draws per arm (maximum_model_calls allowed by the contract = 600). The provider-call audit in the execution manifest records stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300 and model_calls_used = 300.

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded = the same shared candidate validated by deterministic validators; if any validator reported forbidden reachability, the preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair LLM call per pair. Across the run no repair prompt was issued because validators never reported forbidden reachability; per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false in the archived scoring artifacts.

Validator set and forbidden-reachability predicate (concise technical definition): Two deterministic validators ran in Dockerized, deterministic orchestration: (1) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that executes/normalizes the candidate configuration against the emulator and checks dynamic execution semantics, and (2) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer that evaluates network-state reachability properties. The scoring rule combined the two validators with a logical OR: a configuration is labeled violating if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate. For this study the forbidden-reachability predicate is the validator-detected emergence of reachability or policy violations that contradict the task-specified protected-interface/workflow constraints (task payloads include protected_interfaces such as 'mgmt1'); concrete per-episode predicate outcomes and validator outputs are archived in execution/scoring/*.json (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0').

Tasks, emulator, and determinism: Tasks are synthetic intent→configuration problems generated deterministically (task_manifest entries include protected_interfaces and workflow_policies); emulation used Dockerized FRRouting-style router images and deterministic orchestration. Exact sampling seeds, task payloads, and orchestration recipes are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl. Deduplication and contamination handling followed the preregistration (exact duplicates removed; fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15 excluded or flagged). Sensitivity analyses for contamination were prespecified though not invoked because no technical failures or missingness occurred.
sections.results:
Execution and provider accounting: The run completed the planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms) with completed_episode_count = 600 and failed_episode_count = 0. Provider-call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate contract shows model_calls_used = 300 (execution/execution_manifest.json). Representative per-task artifacts (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) document the shared-candidate playback and deterministic validator traces.

Primary confirmatory outcome: All 300 matched pairs passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0. Prespecified bootstrap-percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). Because no validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, the preregistered repair policy was never triggered and no repair LLM calls occurred; all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false.

Descriptive upper bound on undetected baseline violations: Observing 0 violations out of N = 300 provides a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the true baseline violation rate of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). This numeric bound quantifies the run's detection sensitivity under the chosen contract and should be interpreted as a descriptive limit rather than confirmatory evidence of verifier effectiveness.

Verifier concordance and repair activity: The two deterministic validators were concordant across all archived episodes (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in the analysis artifacts and per-episode scoring files). Because no forbidden-reachability detections occurred, repair was not exercised; therefore the study does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory hypothesis is untestable here: The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis targeted a paired reduction in forbidden-reachability incidents achievable through verifier-in-the-loop repair. Two coupled design facts rendered that hypothesis untestable in this run: (1) the shared_initial_candidate semantics reduced independent-sample variance between arms by replaying a single initial candidate to both baseline and guarded conditions (this choice conserved provider calls but lowered the chance to observe arm-discordant outcomes), and (2) none of the programmatic adversarial variants triggered validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators. The resulting degenerate contingency (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = 0) leaves no discordant pairs for McNemar-style inference and therefore cannot measure repair efficacy. We state this limitation prominently and quantitatively.

Design lessons and operational recommendations (artifact-grounded): (a) Generation semantics matter: a shared-candidate contract reduces model call cost (model_calls_used = 300) but also the independent variance needed to produce discordant failures that repair could correct; for repair-efficacy evaluations prefer independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or larger sample sizes. (b) Adversary potency matters: the deterministic programmatic adversarial variants used here did not produce validator-detectable violations; stronger or targeted adversaries that probe verifier predicates are required to exercise repair paths. (c) Verifier strength and diversity matter: results depend on the validators used; combining multiple oracle families and production-grade oracles increases the chance of detecting violations that repair can address. (d) Reproducibility is practical: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and the analysis log (including bootstrap parameters and seed = 1729) are archived and permit exact replay of the reported accounting and contingency outcomes.

Threats to validity (artifact-referenced): Internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope (execution/model_configuration.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json show single-model runs and shared generation). Construct validity depends on how well the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators model operational security risk (validator IDs and versions are recorded per episode in execution/scoring/*.json). External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic. Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and the preregistered power assumptions (nonzero baseline violation rate) are not met. All artifact locations cited above permit independent reanalysis and targeted follow-up runs designed to exercise repair behavior.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation under a constrained adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate) with declared model gpt-5-mini and two deterministic validators combined by logical OR. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not invoked and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The principal, artifact-grounded empirical output is a bound on the undetected baseline violation rate under the chosen contract (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994) plus reproducible execution accounting and per-episode validator traces. Follow-up experiments that aim to test repair efficacy should adopt independent-condition generation, stronger adversary constructions, expanded repair budgets, and more diverse verifiers; the archived artifacts here provide a deterministic baseline and budgeting reference for such stress tests.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model (gpt-5-mini), and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead (model_calls_used = 300) but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
